fixtures.rationale: The deprecation provides consumers no replacement or migration action.

export function connectLegacy() {}
fixtures.rationale: The comment names a concrete replacement invocation.

fixtures.source: try { await load(); } catch (error) { throw new Error("Load failed"); }
fixtures.rationale: The escaping replacement Error does not preserve the caught error as structured cause data.

fixtures.source: try { await load(); } catch (error) { throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: error }); }
fixtures.rationale: The replacement Error visibly retains the caught error in its cause.
A substring match on human-readable message text determines recovery behavior.

fixtures.source: export async function loadSafely() { try { return await load(); } catch (error) { logger.error(error.message); throw error; } }
fixtures.rationale: The message is emitted for reporting and does not choose control flow.

fixtures.source: export async function loadSafely() { try { return await load(); } catch (error) { logger.info("Do not parse error.message here"); throw error; } }
fixtures.rationale: The text error.message appears only inside a string literal and is not a member access or dispatch operation.

fixtures.source: export async function loadSafely() { try { return await load(); } catch (error) { if (/timed out/iu.test(error.message)) return retry(); throw error; } }
fixtures.rationale: The regular expression tests the caught error's message and uses the result to select retry behavior.

fixtures.source: export function record(order: Order) { span.addEvent(`order.${order.id}`); }
fixtures.rationale: The event name embeds an occurrence-specific order identifier.

fixtures.source: export function record(order: Order) { span.addEvent("order.completed", { orderId: order.id }); }
fixtures.rationale: The stable event name keeps the order identifier in attributes.

fixtures.source: try { await charge(); } catch (error) { logger.error(error); telemetry.captureException(error); throw error; }
fixtures.rationale: Two visible reporting sinks emit the same caught exception in one boundary.

fixtures.source: try { await migrate(); } catch (error) { logger.error(error); telemetry.captureException(error); }
fixtures.rationale: Both sinks receive the exception, but the bounded source does not establish whether dual emission is required during migration.

fixtures.source: try { await charge(); } catch (error) { logger.error("error while charging"); telemetry.captureException(new ChargeError("error")); throw error; }
fixtures.rationale: Neither reporting call receives the caught exception; the catch binding appears only in string literals.

fixtures.source: try { await charge(); } catch (error) { logger.error({ error, operation: "charge" }); telemetry.captureException(error); throw error; }
fixtures.rationale: The same caught exception is sent first as structured log data and then directly to exception telemetry.

export function recentFailures() { return db.job.findMany({ where: { failed: true }, take: 100 }); }
fixtures.rationale: The one-shot bounded failure lookup uses take as a safety cap, not for page traversal.

fixtures.source: export async function read() { const a = await open("a"); const b = await open("b"); await a.close(); await b.close(); }
fixtures.rationale: Failure acquiring or closing the second resource can prevent complete cleanup.
Nested finally blocks ensure the first resource is cleaned if later acquisition, work, or cleanup fails.

fixtures.source: export async function run() { return retry(() => request(), { retries: 3, delay: 100 }); }
fixtures.rationale: Multiple attempts use a fixed delay without progressive backoff or randomization.

fixtures.source: export async function run() { return retry(() => request(), { retries: 3, backoff: "exponential", jitter: true }); }
fixtures.rationale: The retry options visibly combine exponential backoff with jitter.

fixtures.source: export async function run() { return retry(() => request(), { retries: 3 }); }
fixtures.rationale: A finite attempt count does not bound total elapsed time when an attempt can hang.

fixtures.source: export async function run() { return retry(() => request(), { retries: 3, totalTimeoutMs: 5000 }); }
fixtures.rationale: A visible total-timeout option spans all retry attempts.

fixtures.source: export function run(req: Request) { return exec(req.body.command); }
fixtures.rationale: Request-controlled command text flows directly to a shell execution sink.
The executable is fixed, shell parsing is disabled, and request input selects from a visible argument allowlist.

fixtures.source: export function update(req: Request) { return accounts.update(req.params.id, req.body); }
fixtures.rationale: The entire request body is passed to persistence without a field allowlist.

fixtures.source: export function update(req: Request) { const { displayName, biography } = req.body; return accounts.update(req.params.id, { displayName, biography }); }
fixtures.rationale: Only two visibly allowlisted client-mutable fields reach persistence.

fixtures.source: export function continueTo(req: Request, res: Response) { res.redirect(req.query.next); }
fixtures.rationale: Request data directly determines the redirect target without a local-path or origin restriction.

fixtures.source: export function continueTo(req: Request, res: Response) { const target = new URL(req.query.next, "https://app.example"); if (target.origin !== "https://app.example") throw new Error("bad redirect"); res.redirect(target.toString()); }
fixtures.rationale: The parsed target must match the exact allowed origin before redirecting.

fixtures.source: test("rejects malformed JSON", () => { assert.throws(() => parsePayload("{")); });
fixtures.rationale: The test promises a distinguishable malformed-input failure but accepts any thrown error.

fixtures.source: test("rejects malformed JSON", () => { assert.throws(() => parsePayload("{"), SyntaxError); });
fixtures.rationale: The assertion checks the stable error class promised by the test.

fixtures.source: test("becomes ready", async () => { startWork(); await sleep(500); expect(status()).toBe("ready"); });
fixtures.rationale: A fixed real-time sleep guesses when work is ready before checking status.

fixtures.source: test("fires after timeout", async () => { vi.useFakeTimers(); setTimeout(markFired, 500); await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(500); expect(fired()).toBe(true); });
fixtures.rationale: The test advances controlled virtual time to verify timeout behavior rather than sleeping for readiness.

fixtures.source: test("documents a timer fixture", () => { const fixture = `setTimeout(resolve, 500)`; expect(fixture).toContain("setTimeout"); });
fixtures.rationale: A timer call quoted inside fixture text is not executable synchronization.

A transaction stamped five minutes before the real clock falls into the previous month when the suite runs just after midnight on the first, so the month-to-date total becomes zero.
The expected key and the code under test each read the wall clock separately, so a run that straddles a month rollover compares two different periods.
The entry's creation time comes from the real clock while the release time is a fixed literal, so once the wall clock passes that literal the comparison flips and the test fails on every run.
The test computes tomorrow from one wall-clock read while daysUntil reads the clock again, so a run across midnight or a daylight-saving change counts a different number of days.
The boundary case is built from the real date, so leap days and runs across midnight move the birthday off the exact threshold the test claims to check.
The rendered receipt embeds the current time, so the snapshot cannot match on any later run.
A real elapsed-time budget depends on machine load, so the same code passes or fails with CI contention.
The service uses its default real clock and the expectation reads the clock again, so the two values disagree when the run crosses a month boundary.
Fake timers pin the system time mid-month before any clock read, so every new Date() in the test is deterministic.
Date.now is mocked to a fixed instant before either read, so the expiry check does not depend on the wall clock.
Luxon's clock source is pinned to a fixed instant before the code under test and the expectation read DateTime.now.
The service and the transaction both take time from an injected fixed clock, so the test never reads the wall clock.
Every date is a fixed literal, so no clock is read.

The imported helper may build the service on a frozen clock, but its implementation is not visible, so whether both reads agree is unknown.
